text: Kenneth Daniel Ball (22 May 1930 – 7 March 2013) was an English jazz musician best known as the bandleader, lead trumpet player, and vocalist in Kenny Ball and His Jazzmen. Born in Ilford, Essex, Ball left school at age 14 to work as a clerk in an advertising agency but began taking trumpet lessons simultaneously. He started as a semi-professional sideman in various bands while also working as a salesman and at the advertising agency, turning professional in 1953 and playing with bands led by Sid Phillips, Charlie Galbraith, Eric Delaney, and Terry Lightfoot before forming his own trad jazz band, Kenny Ball and His Jazzmen, in 1958. His Dixieland band was central to the early 1960s UK jazz revival. In 1961, their recording of Cole Porter's "Samantha" (Pye 7NJ.2040 – released February 1961) became a hit, reaching No. 2 on the UK Singles Chart by the end of 1961 and No. 1 on the Hot 100 in March 1962 with "Midnight in Moscow" (Pye 7NJ.2049 – released November 1961), which sold over one million copies and earned gold disc status. Their next single, "March of the Siamese Children" (Pye 7NJ.2051 – released February 1962), from The King and I, topped the New Musical Express chart on 9 March 1962. Their popularity in the UK led to Ball being featured alongside Cliff Richard, Brenda Lee, Joe Brown, Craig Douglas, and Frank Ifield on the NME cover in July 1962, although in the United States they remained a "one-hit wonder." Ball appeared with his band in the 1962 British musical film It's Trad, Dad!, directed by Richard Lester. In January 1963, NME reported that the largest trad jazz event in Britain had taken place at Alexandra Palace, featuring George Melly, Diz Disley, Acker Bilk, Chris Barber, Alex Welsh, Ken Colyer, Monty Sunshine, Bob Wallis, Bruce Turner, Mick Mulligan, and Ball. That same year, Ball was awarded honorary citizenship of New Orleans and appeared in the 1963 film Live It Up!, starring Gene Vincent. In 1968, the band performed with Louis Armstrong during his final European tour. Ball appeared on BBC Television's Pop Go The Sixties, broadcast on BBC 1 on 31 December 1969, performing "Midnight in Moscow" with his Jazzmen. He made guest appearances on every edition of the first six series of the BBC's Morecambe and Wise Show, and later stated that the peak of his career was when Kenny Ball and His Jazzmen performed at the wedding reception of Prince Charles and Lady Diana. Ball and his band enjoyed one of the longest unbroken spells of success for trad jazz bands, with his status comparable to that of Acker Bilk and Chris Barber. Their joint album, The Best of Ball, Barber and Bilk, reached No. 1 on the UK Albums Chart. Ball charted fourteen top 40 hit singles in the UK, all released on the Pye record label. In 2001, Ball participated in the recording of an album on the Decca label titled British Jazz Legends Together, featuring Don Lusher, Acker Bilk, John Chilton and the Feetwarmers, John Dankworth, Humphrey Lyttelton, and George Melly. Ball continued touring until shortly before his death, with his last scheduled concert being with Acker Bilk and Chris Barber at Manchester's Bridgewater Hall on 21 February 2013. He died at Basildon Hospital, Essex, where he was being treated for pneumonia. Since 2018, the band has continued as a show titled Kenny Ball's Greatest Hits, produced by trombonist Ian Bateman, who played with the band in its later years as deputy for John Bennett and then under the leadership of Kenny's son, Keith. The show features musicians who were either in Kenny's band or involved in the 3B's shows.
